source_text: Καταφαίνεται τοίνυν προπαιδεία ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ σὺν καὶ αὐτῇ φιλοσοφίᾳ θεόθεν ἥκειν εἰς ἀνθρώπους οὐ κατὰ προηγούμενον, ἀλλ’ ὅν τρόπον οἱ ὑετοὶ καταρρήγνυνται εἰς τὴν γῆν τὴν ἀγαθὴν καὶ εἰς τὴν κοπρίαν καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ δώματα. βλαστάνει δ’ ὁμοίως καὶ πόα καὶ πυρός, φύεται δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν μνημάτων συκῆ καὶ εἴ τι τῶν ἀναιδεστέρων δένδρων, καὶ τὰ φυόμενα ἐν τύπῳ προκύπτει τῶν ἀληθῶν, ὅτι τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ ὑετοῦ ἀπέλαυσε δυνάμεως, ἀλλ’ οὐ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔσχηκε χάριν τοῖς ἐν τῷ πίονι φυεῖσιν ἤτοι ξηρανθέντα ἢ ἀποτιλθέντα. καὶ δὴ κἀνταῦθα χρησιμεύει ἡ τοῦ σπόρου παραβολή, ἣν ὁ κύριος ἡρμήνευσεν. εἷς γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἐν ἀνθρώποις γῆς γεωργὸς ὁ ἄνωθεν σπείρων ἐκ καταβολῆς κόσμου τὰ θρεπτικὰ σπέρματα, ὁ τὸν κύριον καθ’ ἕκαστον καιρὸν ἐπομβρίσας λόγον, οἱ καιροὶ δὲ καὶ οἱ τόποι οἱ δεκτικοὶ τὰς διαφορὰς ἐγέννησαν. ἄλλως τε ὁ γεωργὸς οὐ πυροὺς μόνον (καίτοι καὶ τούτων πλείους εἰσι διαφοραί), σπείρει δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα σπέρματα, κριθάς τε καὶ κυάμους καὶ πίσον καὶ ἄρακα καὶ τὰ κηπευόμενα καὶ τὰ ἀνθητικὰ σπέρματα· τῆς αὐτῆς δὲ γεωργίας καὶ ἡ φυτουργία, ἐργάζεσθαι ὅσα εἰς αὐτά τε τὰ φυτώρια καὶ εἰς παραδείσους καὶ τὰ ὡραῖα καὶ ὅλως παντοίων δένδρων φύσιν καὶ τροφήν. ὡσαύτως δὲ οὐχ ἡ ποιμενικὴ μόνη, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ βουκολικὴ ἱπποτροφική τε καὶ κυνοτροφικὴ καὶ μελισσουργικὴ τέχναι πᾶσαι, συνελόντι δ’ εἰπεῖν ἀγελοκομική τε καὶ ζῳοτροφικὴ ἀλλήλων μὲν τῷ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον διαφέρουσι, πλὴν αἱ πᾶσαι βιωφελεῖς. φιλοσοφίαν δὲ οὐ τὴν Στωικὴν λέγω οὐδὲ τὴν Πλατωνικὴν ἢ τὴν Ἐπικούρειόν τε καὶ Ἀριστοτελικήν, ἀλλ’ ὅσα εἴρηται παρ’ ἑκάστῃ τῶν αἱρέσεων τούτων καλῶς, δικαιοσύνην μετὰ εὐσεβοῦς ἐπιστήμης ἐκδιδάσκοντα, τοῦτο σύμπαν τὸ ἐκλεκτικὸν φιλοσοφίαν φημί. ὅσα δὲ ἀνθρωπίνων λογισμῶν ἀποτεμόμενοι παρεχάραξαν, ταῦτα οὐκ ἄν ποτε θεῖα εἴποιμ’ ἄν. Ἤδη δὲ κἀκεῖνο σκοπῶμεν, ὡς εἴ ποτε οἱ μὴ ἐπιστάμενοι διαβιοῦσι καλῶς † εὖ ποιεῖν· εὐποιίᾳ γὰρ περιπεπτώκασιν, ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ εὐστοχοῦσι διὰ συνέσεως εἰς τὸν περὶ ἀληθείας λόγον, Ἀβραὰμ δὲ οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη, ἀλλ’ ἐκ πίστεως. οὐδὲν οὖν ὄφελος αὐτοῖς μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν τοὺ βίον, κἂν εὐεργεῖς ὦσι νῦν, εἰ μὴ πίστιν ἔχοιεν. διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ Ἑλλήνων φωνῇ ἡρμηνεύθησαν αἱ γραφαί, ὡς μὴ πρόφασιν ἀγνοίας προβάλλεσθαι δυνηθῆναί ποτε αὐτούς, οἵους τε ὄντας ἐπακοῦσαι καὶ τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν, ἢν μόνον ἐθελήσωσιν. ἄλλως τις περὶ ἀληθείας λέγει, ἄλλως ἡ ἀλήθεια ἑαυτὴν ἑρμηνεύει. ἕτερον στοχασμὸς ἀληθείας, ἕτερον ἡ ἀλήθεια, ἄλλο ὁμοίωσις, ἄλλο αὐτὸ τὸ ὄν, καὶ ἣ μὲν μαθήσει καὶ ἀσκήσει περιγίνεται, ἣ δὲ δυνάμει καὶ πίστει. δωρεὰ γὰρ ἡ διδασκαλία τῆς θεοσεβείας, χάρις δὲ ἡ πίστις. ποιοῦντες γὰρ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ θέλημα γινώσκομεν. ἀνοίξατε οὖν, φησὶν ἡ γραφή, πύλας δικαιοσύνης, ἵνα ἐν αὐταῖς εἰσελθὼν ἐξομολογήσωμαι τῷ κυρίῳ. ἀλλ’ αἱ μὲν εἰς μὲν εἰς δικαιοσύνην ὁδοί, πολυτρόπως σῴζοντος τοῦ θεοῦ (ἀγαθὸς γάρ), πολλαί τε καὶ ποικίλαι καὶ φέρουσαι εἰς τὴν κυρίαν ὁδόν τε καὶ πύλην. ἐὰν δὲ τὴν βασιλικήν τε καὶ αὐθεντικὴν εἴσοδον ζητῇς, ἀκούσῃ· αὕτη ἡ πύλη τοῦ κυρίου, δίκαιοι εἰσελεύσονται ἐν αὐτῇ. πολλῶν τοίνυν ἀνεῳγμένων πυλῶν ἡ ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ αὕτη ἦν ἐν Χριστῷ, ἐν ᾗ μακάριοι πάντες οἱ εἰσελθόντες καὶ κατευθύνοντες τὴν πορείαν αὐτῶν ἐν ὁσιότητι γνωστικῇ. αὐτίκα ὁ Κλήμης ἐν τῇ πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολῇ κατὰ λέξιν φησὶ τὰς διαφορὰς ἐκτιθέμενος τῶν κατὰ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν δοκίμων· ἤτω τις πιστός, ἤτω δυνατὸς γνῶσιν ἐξειπεῖν, ἤτω σοφὸς ἐν διακρίσει λόγων, ἤτω γοργὸς ἐν ἔργοις.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, it is evident that Hellenic pre-education, along with philosophy, comes from God to humans, not in a predetermined manner, but in the way that rains pour down on the good earth and on the dung heap and on the roofs. And it sprouts similarly, both grass and wheat, and a fig tree grows even on tombs, and if any of the more shameless trees, and the things that grow in a type, it becomes clear from the true things, that they have enjoyed the same power of the rain, but they have not had the same grace to those who have grown in the fat soil, either having withered or having fallen. And indeed, the parable of the seed is also useful here, which the Lord interpreted. For there is one farmer of the earth that is in humans, who sows the nourishing seeds from the foundation of the world, who at each time pours down the word of the Lord, and the times and the places that receive them have produced the differences. In another way, the farmer does not sow only wheat (and yet there are many differences even among these), but also sows other seeds, barley and beans and peas and pulse and the seeds that are cultivated in gardens and the flowering seeds; and of the same farming, there is also the cultivation of trees, working on all the things that pertain to the nurseries and the paradises and the beautiful things and, in general, the nature and nourishment of all kinds of trees. Similarly, it is not only the pastoral art, but also the art of cattle breeding and horse breeding and dog breeding and beekeeping, and to say it briefly, all the arts of herding and animal breeding, which differ from each other in more or less, but are all beneficial for life. But I do not mean the Stoic philosophy or the Platonic or the Epicurean and Aristotelian, but all that has been said well by each of these sects, teaching righteousness with pious knowledge, this I call the eclectic philosophy. But the things that, having cut off human reasonings, they have gone beyond, these I would not say are divine. Now, let us also consider this, that if those who do not know live well, they do well by chance; for some have also hit the mark of the truth through their consciousness, but Abraham was justified not by works, but by faith. Therefore, this life is of no benefit to them after death, even if they are benefactors now, if they do not have faith. For this reason, the scriptures were interpreted in the language of the Greeks, so that they might not have an excuse for ignorance, being able to hear also the things from us, if only they wish. One thing is the speculation about truth, another thing is the truth itself, one thing is the likeness, another thing is the reality, and one is acquired by learning and practice, the other by power and faith. For the teaching of piety is a gift, and faith is a grace. For by doing the will of God, we come to know his will. Therefore, the scripture says, 'Open the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and confess to the Lord.' But the ways to righteousness are many, since God saves in many ways (for he is good), and they are varied and lead to the main road and gate. But if you seek the royal and authentic entrance, listen: 'This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter through it.' Therefore, of the many opened gates, the one in righteousness is in Christ, in which all who enter and direct their journey in gnosis of holiness are blessed. Immediately, Clement, in his epistle to the Corinthians, says literally, setting forth the differences of those who are approved in the church: let someone be faithful, let someone be able to express knowledge, let someone be wise in discerning words, let someone be eager in deeds.

pass_b_english: It is therefore evident that Hellenic pre-education, along with its philosophy, comes from God to humanity not in a predetermined manner, but just as rains pour down upon the good earth and upon the dung heap and upon the roofs alike. Both grass and wheat sprout similarly, and a fig tree even springs up on tombs, along with any of the more shameless trees; the things that grow show in a figure what is true, demonstrating that they have all enjoyed the same power of the rain, yet they have not received the same grace as those growing in rich soil, for they either wither or are plucked up. The parable of the seed, which the Lord interpreted, is useful here as well. For there is one Farmer of the earth that exists in humans, who has been sowing the nourishing seeds from the foundation of the world, who rains down the Word of the Lord at each appointed time, and the times and places that receive them have produced the differences. Moreover, the Farmer does not sow wheat alone — though even among these there are many varieties — but also sows the other seeds: barley, beans, peas, pulse, the cultivated garden seeds, and the flowering seeds; and of the same husbandry is the cultivation of trees, working upon all that pertains to nurseries, gardens, beautiful plants, and in general the nature and nourishment of all kinds of trees. Likewise, it is not only the pastoral art, but also the arts of cattle-breeding, horse-breeding, dog-breeding, and beekeeping; to sum up, all the arts of herding and animal husbandry, which differ from one another in degree, yet are all beneficial for life. When I speak of philosophy, I do not mean the Stoic, the Platonic, the Epicurean, or the Aristotelian systems, but rather whatever has been well said by each of these schools, teaching righteousness with pious knowledge; this whole eclectic compilation I call philosophy. But the things which, having cut off human reasonings, they have gone beyond, I would not ever call divine. Now let us consider this also: if those who do not know live well, they do well by chance; for some have even hit upon the truth through understanding, yet Abraham was justified not by works but by faith. There is therefore no benefit to them after the end of life, even if they are benefactors now, if they do not have faith. For this reason the Scriptures were interpreted in the language of the Greeks, so that they might not be able to put forward an excuse of ignorance, since they are capable of hearing also the things from us, if only they are willing. One thing is speculation about truth, another is truth itself; one thing is a likeness, another is the reality; one is acquired by learning and practice, the other by power and faith. For the teaching of piety is a gift, and faith is a grace. For by doing the will of God we come to know His will. Therefore Scripture says, ‘Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter through them and give thanks to the Lord’ (Psalm 118:19). But the ways that lead to righteousness are many, since God saves in many ways (for He is good), numerous and varied, and they bear toward the main road and gate. But if you seek the royal and authoritative entrance, hear: ‘This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it’ (Psalm 118:20). Therefore, of the many opened gates, the one in righteousness is in Christ, in which all who enter and direct their journey in gnostic holiness are blessed. Immediately Clement, in his epistle to the Corinthians, states literally, setting forth the distinctions of those approved in the church: let someone be faithful, let someone be able to express knowledge, let someone be wise in discerning words, let someone be eager in deeds.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex agricultural metaphors and the distinction between 'learning/practice' and 'power/faith'. Scripture citations (Psalm 118:19, 118:20) were correctly identified and added to Pass B as required by the instructions for identifying alluded verses. All clauses in the Greek are accounted for in both Pass A and B.
